Explanation

Your application has hardcoded URLs that might correspond to services that are not accessible on Azure.

Review and ensure that the application is attempting to access URLs that would be available from Azure. You might need to migrate those services to Azure too, this way you will get the benefit of lower latency in the cloud.

If your application needs to depend on services that run on-premises, you can connect your Azure and local networks with ExpressRoute, Hybrid Connections, or VPN solutions.
SQL database connection detected
 Potential 3
FilePosition
src\eShopWCFService\Web.config

Explanation

SQL database connection detected.

Ensure the database is available/reachable on Azure.

If it is not, there are multiple ways you can move your data to Azure:
1. Migrate to Azure SQL Database.
2. Consider Azure SQL Managed Instance if you need features that are not available in Azure SQL Database and you don’t want to use a VM.
3. Migrate your database servers directly to SQL Server on Azure VMs.

To assess database migration effort, you can use Azure Migrate tool, see the link below.
Local or network IO operations detected
 Potential 3
FilePosition
src\eShopWinForms\Views\CatalogView.csLine 57

Explanation

Your application has local or network IO operations.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, move persistent I/O to storage mounts (Azure Files/UNC). Keep local writes to temp only; connect to external dependencies via private endpoints/VNet to reduce latency.

IO operations outside of the application folder might not be available on Azure App Service. Review and ensure IO APIs are attempting to access paths that will be available when your app is running on App Service sandbox. If you choose the containerized hosting option, your scenario still might be broken or have scalability issues.

Possible solutions:
1. Files that the application needs can be deployed with the application or put in Azure Storage. You can use Azure Storage File Shares as a drop-in replacement for on-premises file share.
2. Other services that the application depends on might need to be migrated to Azure, this way you will get the benefit of lower latency in the cloud.
3. If your application needs to depend on services that run on-premise, you can connect your Azure and local networks with ExpressRoute, Hybrid Connections, or VPN solutions.
Local OS environment access detected
 Potential 1
FilePosition
src\eShopWinForms\Views\CatalogView.csLine 56

Explanation

Local OS environment access detected.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, Read config via App Settings or App Configuration; avoid machine‑specific environment APIs. Persist environment setup via install scripts when needed.

When running in Azure App Service environment, your application can read environment variables that you define in App Service settings. Using environment API other than reading environment variables might indicate that your application depends on some local machine's features and might be broken on App Service sandbox or not scale well. Review your scenarios and either refactor them to be more cloud friendly or choose the option in App Service to host your application in the sandbox for Windows Container Web Apps.

If you choose to use other Azure hosting options such as Azure Container Apps (ACA) or Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), environment APIs might work, however scaling still might be an issue.
Upgrade to newer target framework to get better cloud experience
 Optional 3
FilePosition
src\eShopWCFService\eShopWCFService.csproj
src\eShopWinForms\eShopWinForms.csproj

Explanation

Upgrade to newer target framework to get better cloud experience.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, validate on .NET Framework 4.8 or move to .NET 10. Persist any runtime prerequisites via install scripts; test in staging before production.

While if targeting other Azure compute services:

Application targeting .NET framework lower than 4.7.1 might missing features that would be needed for some cloud scenarios like scaling or getting secrets from secure external sources.

Azure App Service runs apps on .NET Framework 4.8 or .NET Framework 3.5. Apps running on on .NET Framework versions older than .NET Framework 4.8 could have potential compatibility issues. It is recommended to test your application running on .NET Framework 4.8. Note that it is not necessary to re-target to .NET Framework 4.8, only to validate that the app correctly runs on that version of .NET Framework.

In the long term it is also recommended to upgrade your application to latest supported .NET 8+ which would significantly increase performance of your application. Use tools like .NET Upgrade Assistant to help with upgrading your application to newer .NET.
Connection strings without configuration builders detected
 Optional 3
FilePosition
src\eShopWCFService\Web.config
src\eShopWCFService\Web.config

Explanation

Connection strings without configuration builders detected.

Keeping connection strings directly in the app is not the best practice and might introduce security risks, increased maintenance, scalability challenges or compliance standards (such as PCI DSS, GDPR, etc.).

Instead, it is recommended to use configuration builders to get secrets from secure sources in Azure environment.
System.Data.SqlClient dependency detected
 Optional 3
FilePosition
src\eShopWCFService\Web.config

Explanation

System.Data.SqlClient dependency is detected.

While System.Data.SqlClient will work in Azure, the newer Microsoft.Data.SqlClient package is the primary .NET SQL client moving forward and receiving the latest features. For example, Microsoft.Data.SqlClient easily allows use of Azure Managed Identity from a connection string.

Explanation

Static content detected.

Your current approach of serving static content directly might lead to increased costs, performance issues, maintenance challenges (requiring application redeployment for content changes), and security risks.

Consider moving static content to Azure Blob Storage and adding Azure CDN.

WCF Client APIs
 Mandatory 1
FilePosition

Explanation

WCF client-side APIs for building service clients that communicate with WCF services. These APIs are available as exact equivalents via NuGet packages - add System.ServiceModel.* NuGet packages (System.ServiceModel.Http, System.ServiceModel.Primitives, System.ServiceModel.NetTcp, etc.)
Legacy Configuration System
 Mandatory 2
FilePosition

Explanation

Legacy XML-based configuration system (app.config/web.config) that has been replaced by a more flexible configuration model in .NET Core. The old system was rigid and XML-based. Migrate to Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration with JSON/environment variables; use System.Configuration.ConfigurationManager NuGet package as interim bridge if needed.
GDI+ / System.Drawing
 Mandatory 1
FilePosition

Explanation

System.Drawing APIs for 2D graphics, imaging, and printing that are available via NuGet package System.Drawing.Common. Note: Not recommended for server scenarios due to Windows dependencies; consider cross-platform alternatives like SkiaSharp or ImageSharp for new code.
Windows Forms Legacy Controls
 Mandatory 3
FilePosition

Explanation

Legacy Windows Forms controls that have been removed from .NET Core/5+ including StatusBar, DataGrid, ContextMenu, MainMenu, MenuItem, and ToolBar. These controls were replaced by more modern alternatives. Use ToolStrip, MenuStrip, ContextMenuStrip, and DataGridView instead.
Windows Forms
 Mandatory 1
FilePosition

Explanation

Windows Forms APIs for building Windows desktop applications with traditional Forms-based UI that are available in .NET on Windows. Enable Windows Desktop support: Option 1 (Recommended): Target net9.0-windows; Option 2: Add <UseWindowsDesktop>true</UseWindowsDesktop>; Option 3 (Legacy): Use Microsoft.NET.Sdk.WindowsDesktop SDK.

Explanation

CVE-2024-21907, HIGH. Newtonsoft.Json 6.0.4 is declared in packages.config:5 and referenced by the WinForms project at line 64; affected range <13.0.1, first patched 13.0.1. Upgrade to a supported patched release after compatibility testing. Malicious deeply nested JSON can exhaust the parser stack if attacker-controlled JSON reaches deserialization. Dependency presence is confirmed, but remote JSON reachability is not established; the WCF interface uses SOAP. Withdrawn duplicate GHSA-8rfx-6mr3-5jh3 excluded. Coverage: dotnet list package --include-transitive --format json failed (missing Microsoft.WebApplication.targets, exit 1); packages.config and both csproj HintPaths examined instead. Three distinct declared NuGet packages checked against advisory DB: EntityFramework 6.1.3, Microsoft.AspNet.WebApi.Client 5.2.3, Newtonsoft.Json 6.0.4. No advisory returned for the other two. Transitive inventory incomplete; framework/OS and unmanaged binary vulnerabilities are not covered.

Data Storage & External Services

The server owns a single configured catalog database; the desktop consumes its SOAP contract rather than connecting directly in the observed startup path. Pictures are read from a relative local assets directory, not an image service (src\eShopWinForms\Program.cs:22-26; src\eShopWinForms\Views\CatalogView.cs:48-61). No broker, remote cache, or third-party integration is evidenced in the active path. Actual deployed hosts, database engine version, and availability are unknown.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • Manual composition: Program creates the view, generated proxy, and controller; the controller receives interfaces through its constructor, without an observed DI container (src\eShopWinForms\Program.cs:22-26; src\eShopWinForms\Controllers\CatalogController.cs:14-20).
  • Business service queries EF directly; there is no separate repository layer. A default constructor creates its context, while an overload accepts one (src\eShopWCFService\CatalogService.svc.cs:16-25,56-82).
  • EF entities also serve as mutable WCF data contracts, coupling persistence and wire models (src\eShopWCFService\Models\CatalogItem.cs:10-35).

API & Service Communication Contracts

The observed API is one WCF SOAP endpoint exposing 10 operations, with synchronous request/reply calls from a desktop client. These are not REST resources; the checked-in WSDL and generated proxy are available but show a filter-nullability discrepancy with current server source.

All citations are relative to eShopLegacyNTier; deployed availability is unknown.

These are service-level entities reused on the wire; no gateway DTO or aggregation service exists in the observed flow. See data-architecture.md for fields. WCF uses XML data-contract serialization; WSDL/XSD documents are checked in, not OpenAPI or protobuf (src\eShopWinForms\eShopWinForms.csproj:122-130,258-264).

Contract drift: the generated client accepts nullable filter integers, and its XSD marks them nillable; the current service requires non-nullable int and treats zero as “All” (src\eShopWinForms\Connected Services\eShopServiceReference\Reference.cs:513-517; src\eShopWinForms\Connected Services\eShopServiceReference\CatalogService.xsd:31-35; src\eShopWCFService\ICatalogService.cs:20; src\eShopWCFService\CatalogService.svc.cs:56-62). The desktop passes integers; null interoperability and live WSDL agreement are unverified.

Communication Patterns

  • Synchronous SOAP: desktop controller calls the generated WCF proxy directly; generated Task methods are alternate client invocation methods, not messaging or asynchronous business processing (src\eShopWinForms\Controllers\CatalogController.cs:35-54,75-84; src\eShopWinForms\Connected Services\eShopServiceReference\Reference.cs:501-557).
  • Composition: the controller fetches items and a discount separately, then passes both to the view. This is client-side composition, not gateway aggregation (src\eShopWinForms\Controllers\CatalogController.cs:75-84).
  • Resilience: no explicit retries, circuit breaker, bulkhead, custom timeout values, or downstream-outage fallback is observed. The binding is empty, so framework defaults apply; deployed effective values were not verified (src\eShopWinForms\App.config:21-28). Controller calls have no catch/recovery path.
  • Addressing: a configured development URL is used, with no observed service discovery or client-side load balancing (src\eShopWinForms\App.config:26-28). The server/database must be usable before initial desktop loading; see configuration-inventory.md.
  • Security posture: the configured desktop endpoint is HTTP with basicHttpBinding and no explicit credentials/security mode. The source contract and implementation show no application authorization checks. Server HTTPS protocol mapping and metadata flags exist, but do not establish TLS enforcement, a certificate, or IIS authentication settings (src\eShopWCFService\Web.config:22-42; src\eShopWCFService\eShopWCFService.csproj:20-22,124). Actual host-level access controls remain unknown; do not infer public Internet exposure.
  • Errors: exception details in SOAP faults are disabled; no declared typed business faults or compensating action is observed (src\eShopWCFService\Web.config:29; src\eShopWCFService\ICatalogService.cs:12-34).

Core Business Workflows

Users browse merchandise by brand/type, see date-based promotional prices, inspect dated stock availability, and record shipment availability. No checkout, ordering, payment, or customer-management workflow is evidenced in the assessed application.

All citations are relative to eShopLegacyNTier; flows describe source behavior rather than verified live execution.

The server is the data source of truth; desktop composition does not create a separate domain owner.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Browse and filter promotional catalog

  1. On launch, the controller sets itself on the view, checks promotions, loads all catalog items, loads brand/type filters, then prepares shipment selectors (src\eShopWinForms\Controllers\CatalogController.cs:150-157).
  2. Changing either selector emits a filter event; the controller clears and reloads the grid using the All-filter rule (src\eShopWinForms\Views\CatalogView.cs:106-135; src\eShopWinForms\Controllers\CatalogController.cs:27-29,75-84).
  3. Server returns matching products; controller separately fetches today's discount using the Active-promotion rule, then passes both to the view (src\eShopWCFService\CatalogService.svc.cs:28-30,56-62).
  4. View computes promotional display prices using the Display-price rule and loads local pictures (src\eShopWinForms\Views\CatalogView.cs:48-61). Prices are not persisted back as discounted amounts.
  5. A banner is set only when the initial promotion check finds a discount. A null promotion means zero display discount; it is not an outage fallback (src\eShopWinForms\Controllers\CatalogController.cs:60-69,79-84).

Workflow 2: Record dated shipment availability

  1. User selects a product and enters quantity/date. The form applies the Shipment-input rule and emits an availability event (src\eShopWinForms\Views\CatalogView.cs:157-167).
  2. Controller builds a stock request and submits it synchronously (src\eShopWinForms\Controllers\CatalogController.cs:35-42).
  3. Server applies the Stock-overwrite rule: updates the first matching product/day record, otherwise creates a row using the Application-key rule, then saves (src\eShopWCFService\CatalogService.svc.cs:99-117).
  4. Only after the call returns does the controller notify success; the view displays a message and clears inputs (src\eShopWinForms\Controllers\CatalogController.cs:42-43; src\eShopWinForms\Views\CatalogView.cs:189-195).

Despite UI wording “shipment,” recording an existing day replaces its quantity; it does not increment stock or model shipment movement.

Workflow 3: Check stock availability

  1. User selects a product and calendar day; the form parses the selected product label and raises a search event (src\eShopWinForms\Views\CatalogView.cs:142-151).
  2. Controller queries the service; server applies the Date-availability rule (src\eShopWinForms\Controllers\CatalogController.cs:50-54; src\eShopWCFService\CatalogService.svc.cs:90-96).
  3. The result is appended to the display history with item/date; previous displayed results are not refreshed automatically (src\eShopWinForms\Views\CatalogView.cs:173-182).

Workflow 4: Initialize business reference data

For a missing database, the initializer seeds types, brands, products, dated availability and historical promotions in order. Each category is saved separately (src\eShopWCFService\Models\Infrastructure\CatalogDBInitializer.cs:11-79). Promotions in the checked-in seed all date to 2017; an unmodified seed does not imply an active current promotion (src\eShopWCFService\Models\Infrastructure\PreconfiguredData.cs:41-50).

Catalog create/update/remove operations also exist on the service, but the observed desktop controller does not wire product-maintenance actions (src\eShopWCFService\ICatalogService.cs:27-32; src\eShopWinForms\Controllers\CatalogController.cs:14-20).

Cross-Service Data Flows

There is one desktop-to-server boundary, not multiple independent business services. The desktop fetches item lists and promotion data separately and combines them for display; reference lists populate filter labels. Product image filenames are resolved to local images. Stock submissions carry a logical product ID across the boundary; availability queries return only a quantity (src\eShopWinForms\Controllers\CatalogController.cs:35-54,75-143; src\eShopWinForms\Views\CatalogView.cs:55-61).

No gateway, broker, event choreography, circuit breaker, cached outage fallback, or compensation flow is observed. “No promotion” yields ordinary undiscounted pricing; service failure has no explicit recovery branch in the controller. There is no business authorization or resource-ownership check in the reviewed implementation (src\eShopWCFService\CatalogService.svc.cs:28-117).

Caching Strategy

No explicit cache provider, TTL, eviction policy, second-level cache, or distributed/session cache is configured in src\eShopWCFService\Web.config:52-64 or the data access implementation. Data Ownership Boundaries

The single server context owns catalog reference data, products, dated availability and promotions in one database; there is no evidence of database-per-domain isolation or CQRS. The desktop reads and writes through WCF, not cross-service database joins. Client-side composition pairs catalog items with a global discount; it is not a distributed aggregate (src\eShopWCFService\EntityModel.cs:18-22; src\eShopWinForms\Controllers\CatalogController.cs:75-84). Image bytes remain local assets, while the DB stores filenames (src\eShopWinForms\Views\CatalogView.cs:55-58).
